items.def: Confirms that the data used by the MLS for training, testing, and prediction is of sufficient quality — includes reviews, statistical techniques (e.g., testing data for bias), EDA of training data, and static and dynamic testing of the data pipeline.
Non-random, unfair differences in treatment based on sensitive attributes like gender, age, or race, which is often unlawful and renders the system discriminatory.

Data bias: defects in the training data (unrepresentativeness, historical skews, deliberate poisoning). Algorithmic bias: defects within the algorithm, model, or development framework that introduce systemic unfairness (e.g., a decision threshold for credit scores in loan approval).

Bias test that generates counterfactuals for sensitive attributes, feeds them to the model, and analyzes whether changing a sensitive attribute changes the results — signaling bias. Also applicable to combinations of sensitive attributes (beware unrealistic counterfactuals).

Determines how closely the characteristics of the datasets used for training, validation, and testing match the real-world data the model will encounter in operation (addresses skewed datasets, missing data, disproportionate feature distributions, inadequate scenario coverage, imbalanced classes).

Verifies whether the data in a dataset adheres to predefined rules or constraints (a logical model of the data that should be satisfied if the data are correct); typically automated as part of the data pipeline.

Data points independently labelled by multiple annotators and compared (a form of back-to-back testing); inter-annotator agreement measured with Cohen's Kappa or simple percentage agreement — low IAA indicates defects in guidelines, ambiguous data, or poor annotation.

items.text: Bias test approaches: reviews of the ML workflow/data preparation; reviews of dataset documentation (collection, annotation, populations represented); static analysis of data-prep and model code (anti-patterns, mishandled sensitive attributes); EDA with visualization/clustering (imbalanced data, skewed distributions, anomalous groupings); dynamic testing with a known unbiased representative dataset (statistically significant outcome differences across sensitive groups — catches bias regardless of origin); label correctness testing; disparate impact analysis.

Data pipeline testing layers: design reviews; component testing (ingestion, transformation scripts, sensor interfaces — code reviews, static analysis, hardware tests; validation rules, error handling, malware/poisoning vulnerabilities); component integration (flow across internal interfaces); system testing (smoke, functional, non-functional load/scalability/security, fault injection with defective data, back-to-back vs training pipeline); system integration (external sources, storage, monitoring, downstream models); testing in production (back-to-back vs previous versions, A/B vs baselines, continuous monitoring); configuration management reviews (correct code versions/configs/datasets across training, testing, production).
Representativeness testing runs BEFORE model training; after deployment, continuously monitor operational input data to detect data drift from training distributions (see 6.1.7).

Dataset constraint types — single-value: Missing, Range, Type. Multi-value: Sum, Count, Duplicate, Useful (an attribute with all-unique values like IDs/timestamps provides no learnable patterns), Outlier. Comparison (across attributes): Greater Than, Correlate.

Label correctness approaches: expert review; multiple annotation with IAA (Cohen's Kappa); risk-based prioritization (ambiguous points, boundary cases, safety-critical data); data distribution analysis vs comparable datasets; automated rule-based tests (e.g., bounding boxes within image boundaries); model loss analysis (high loss → possible mislabeling); model confidence score analysis (low confidence → possibly mislabeled/ambiguous/out-of-distribution). Combine approaches for best results.

blocks.title: Input data risks → mitigations (abbreviated)
rows: Bias from training data defects; systemic unfairness in algorithm/model/framework
Untrustworthy data sources; poorly managed data
A/B testing; Data provenance testing; EDA; red-teaming attacks
Internally inconsistent dataset; out-of-range data; wrong types
Imbalanced/skewed/missing data; subset of use cases; range not covered
Poor labelling guidelines; ambiguous data; poor annotation
Pipeline design/integration failures; quality defects; performance degradation; security breaches

items.text: Define the target population: understand use cases/operational context; analyze end users and environments; identify expected operational distributions and edge cases (domain experts, data from existing systems, benchmark datasets e.g. NIST); apply stratified sampling to reference data to cover all relevant subgroups.

Analyze data characteristics: apply EDA to the datasets under test and the reference dataset (histograms, scatter plots); examine feature relationships and correlations; identify anomalies, gaps, unusual concentrations.
Apply statistical assessment techniques: formal tests such as Chi-squared and Kolmogorov-Smirnov to compare distributions; check class imbalances; verify coverage of typical and edge/boundary cases.
Identify sensitive attributes for the model.
Generate counterfactuals for the sensitive attributes (e.g., gender changed from male to female in a loan application).
Generate model output by presenting it with the counterfactuals.
Analyze results of multiple tests for statistical significance — a change in results when a sensitive attribute changes signals bias.

Data bias originates in the training data (unrepresentative, historically skewed, poisoned); algorithmic bias originates in the algorithm/model/framework (e.g., an unfair decision threshold) — dynamic testing detects output bias regardless of source.

Bias (5.1.2, unfair treatment), pipeline (5.1.3, data flow machinery), representativeness (5.1.4, does data match operational reality), constraints (5.1.5, rule/consistency checks), label correctness (5.1.6, supervision quality); anchor risk→test-type on the 5.1.1 table.

items.confusion: Single-value vs multi-value vs comparison constraints
items.text: Single-value checks one attribute value in one instance (Missing/Range/Type); multi-value checks values across instances (Sum/Count/Duplicate/Useful/Outlier); comparison checks one attribute against another (Greater Than/Correlate).

items.confusion: Chi-squared / Kolmogorov-Smirnov belong to representativeness, not drift testing
items.text: They are the named statistical tests for comparing data distributions in representativeness testing (5.1.4); drift detection is discussed in 6.1.7 — don't mix them in exam answers.
